decks.title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter — Part 1: The photoelectric effect
goals: Describe the observations of Hertz, Hallwachs and Lenard on the photoelectric effect
Interpret graphs of photocurrent against intensity, collector potential and frequency
Explain why the wave theory of light cannot account for the observations

slides.heading: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
slides.body_md: Part 1 — light that knocks electrons out of metals, and four observations the wave theory of light could not explain.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: observations, the experiment, the graphs, the failure of the wave theory, the need for photons

slides.narration: By the end of the nineteenth century light was firmly a wave: it showed interference and diffraction, and Maxwell had explained it as an electromagnetic wave. Then a small effect turned up that waves could not explain. Light falling on a metal can knock electrons out of it. In this part we look at the experiments on this photoelectric effect and the puzzling results they gave.

slides.heading: Electron emission and the work function
slides.body_md: Free electrons in a metal are held in by the attraction of the positive ions. The **least energy** needed to remove an electron from the surface is the **work function** $\varphi_0$, usually given in **electronvolts**: $1\ \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ J.
bullets: Energy can be supplied by heating (**thermionic emission**), a very strong electric field (**field emission**) or light (**photoelectric emission**).
Typical values: caesium about 2.1 eV, potassium about 2.3 eV, zinc about 4.3 eV, platinum about 5.6 eV.

visual.alt: Table of approximate work functions of caesium, potassium, sodium, zinc and platinum in electronvolts

slides.narration: A metal is full of free electrons, but they cannot simply leave: near the surface the positive ions pull them back. The smallest energy that lets an electron escape is the work function. It is usually quoted in electronvolts, the energy an electron gains through one volt, one point six times ten to the minus nineteen joule. Alkali metals like caesium and potassium have small work functions.

slides.heading: Discovery: Hertz, Hallwachs and Lenard
slides.body_md: Early observations:
bullets: **Hertz** (1887): sparks jumped more easily across a gap when its electrodes were lit by **ultraviolet** light.
**Hallwachs**: a **negatively** charged zinc plate lost its charge in ultraviolet light; a neutral plate became **positive**; a positive plate was unaffected.
**Lenard**: ultraviolet on the emitter of an evacuated tube made a **current** flow; it stopped at once when the light was cut off. The particles emitted were **electrons** (photoelectrons).
Zinc and cadmium need ultraviolet; alkali metals respond even to **visible** light.

slides.narration: Hertz noticed that ultraviolet light made sparks jump more easily. Hallwachs found that a negatively charged zinc plate lost its charge in ultraviolet light, while a neutral one became positive, so negative charge was leaving the metal. Lenard showed that light on a plate inside an evacuated tube produced a current, and the particles turned out to be electrons. The light seemed to knock them out.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from stopping potential to speed
slides.body_md: Photoelectrons from a metal are just stopped by a retarding potential of 1.5 V. Find their maximum kinetic energy in eV and in J, and their maximum speed.
bullets: Step 1 — $K_\text{max} = eV_0 = 1.5$ eV $= 1.5 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 2.4 \times 10^{-19}$ J.
Step 2 — $v_\text{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K_\text{max}}{m_e}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 2.4 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}} \approx 7.26 \times 10^{5}$ m s$^{-1}$.

slides.narration: An electron climbing against one and a half volts loses one and a half electronvolts of kinetic energy, so the fastest electrons had exactly that much. Multiply by one point six times ten to the minus nineteen to get joules. Then use half m v squared: the fastest photoelectrons leave at about seven times ten to the five metres per second, a few hundred kilometres every second.

slides.heading: The experimental arrangement
slides.body_md: Light of known **frequency** and **intensity** falls on the emitter C in an evacuated tube. The collector A can be made **positive** (accelerating) or **negative** (retarding) relative to C. A microammeter reads the **photocurrent**.
bullets: Vary one thing at a time: intensity, collector potential, frequency.
The tube is evacuated so that electrons do not collide with air molecules.

slides.narration: In the laboratory version, light passes through a quartz window, which lets ultraviolet through, onto the emitter plate. Photoelectrons cross the vacuum to the collector, and the current is read on a microammeter. A battery with a reversing switch lets us make the collector positive, to pull electrons across, or negative, to push them back. We change one quantity at a time and watch the current.

slides.heading: Effect of intensity
slides.body_md: Keep the frequency (above threshold) and collector potential fixed and vary the intensity:
bullets: The photocurrent is **directly proportional** to the intensity.
So the **number** of photoelectrons emitted per second is proportional to the intensity.

visual.alt: Straight line through the origin: the photocurrent is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident light, for a frequency above threshold

slides.narration: First keep the colour of the light and the collector potential fixed, and make the light brighter. The photocurrent rises in direct proportion. Since each electron carries the same charge, a current twice as large means twice as many electrons leaving every second. Brighter light frees more electrons. So far, nothing surprising.

slides.heading: Effect of potential: stopping potential
slides.body_md:
Make the collector more positive: the current rises to a **saturation** value (all emitted electrons collected). Make it negative: the current falls, and is zero at the **stopping potential** $-V_0$, which stops even the fastest electrons:
$$eV_0 = K_\text{max} = \tfrac{1}{2}m v_\text{max}^2$$
bullets: For one frequency, **different intensities** give **different saturation currents** but the **same** stopping potential.
So $K_\text{max}$ does **not** depend on intensity.

visual.alt: Photocurrent against collector potential for three intensities of light of one frequency: the saturation current rises in proportion to intensity, but all three curves fall to zero at the same stopping potential
visual.caption: Same frequency: saturation current ∝ intensity; stopping potential unchanged.

slides.narration: Now vary the collector potential. With the collector positive, the current levels off at a saturation value once every emitted electron is being collected. Making the collector negative turns electrons back, and at the stopping potential even the fastest ones fail to arrive. Here is the surprise: brighter light gives a larger saturation current, but exactly the same stopping potential. The fastest electrons are no faster in brighter light.

slides.body_md: Choose the correct option.

slides.heading: Effect of frequency
slides.body_md: At the same intensity, **higher frequency** gives a **larger stopping potential**, so a larger $K_\text{max}$. Plotting $V_0$ against $\nu$ gives a **straight line**:
bullets: Below a **threshold frequency** $\nu_0$ there is **no emission at all**, however intense the light.
$\nu_0$ depends on the metal; the slope of the line is the same for all metals.

visual.alt: Stopping potential against frequency for potassium and zinc: two parallel straight lines of slope h over e, cutting the frequency axis at each metal’s threshold frequency
visual.caption: Slope h/e is the same for every metal; the intercept on the ν axis is the threshold frequency ν₀ = φ₀/h.

slides.narration: Finally, change the frequency at constant intensity. Higher frequencies need a larger stopping potential, so the electrons come out with more energy. A graph of stopping potential against frequency is a straight line. It cuts the frequency axis at the threshold frequency, below which no electrons come out at all, however bright the light. Different metals give parallel lines with different thresholds.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Planck’s constant from two readings
slides.body_md: For one metal, light of frequency $8.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz gives $V_0 = 1.32$ V and light of $6.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz gives $V_0 = 0.49$ V. Find the slope of the $V_0$–$\nu$ line, Planck’s constant and the threshold frequency.
bullets: Step 2 — slope $= h/e$, so $h = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 4.15 \times 10^{-15} \approx 6.64 \times 10^{-34}$ J s.
Step 3 — $\nu_0 = 6.0 \times 10^{14} - \dfrac{0.49}{4.15 \times 10^{-15}} \approx 4.82 \times 10^{14}$ Hz; $\varphi_0 = h\nu_0 \approx 2.0$ eV.

visual.alt: Stopping potential against frequency for potassium and zinc: two parallel straight lines of slope h over e, cutting the frequency axis at each metal’s threshold frequency
visual.caption: Slope h/e is the same for every metal; the intercept on the ν axis is the threshold frequency ν₀ = φ₀/h.

slides.narration: The rise in stopping potential divided by the rise in frequency gives the slope, about four point one five times ten to the minus fifteen volt second. That slope is Planck’s constant divided by the electron charge, so multiplying by the charge gives about six point six times ten to the minus thirty four joule second. Working back along the line to zero gives the threshold frequency and a work function of about two electronvolts.

slides.heading: Four observations
slides.body_md: The experiments establish:
bullets: Photocurrent ∝ intensity (for $\nu > \nu_0$).
$K_\text{max}$ (and $V_0$) increase **linearly with frequency** and are **independent of intensity**.
There is a **threshold frequency** $\nu_0$ for each metal.
Emission is **instantaneous**: within about $10^{-9}$ s of the light arriving, even for very dim light.

rows: No emission below a threshold frequency ν₀
Any frequency works if bright enough
One photon must supply at least φ₀ = hν₀
K_max rises with ν, not with intensity
Time lag to absorb enough energy
One photon gives its energy at once

visual.alt: Table comparing four observations of the photoelectric effect with the predictions of the wave theory and the photon picture

slides.narration: Put the results together. The current is proportional to intensity. The maximum kinetic energy grows with frequency but not with intensity. Each metal has a threshold frequency below which nothing happens. And emission starts instantly, within a billionth of a second, even in very faint light. Three of these four observations clash with what we expect of a wave.

- Brighter light → faster electrons
- Any frequency works if intense enough
- Dim light → time lag while energy builds up

**Experiment shows**
- K_max independent of intensity
- No emission below ν₀
- Emission is instantaneous

slides.narration: In nineteen oh five Einstein proposed that light energy comes in packets, later called photons. One equation then explained every photoelectric observation. Twenty years later de Broglie suggested the reverse: if waves can act as particles, particles such as electrons can act as waves. In this part we use Einstein’s equation and calculate the wavelengths of moving particles.

slides.heading: The photon picture
slides.body_md:
Radiation behaves as a stream of **photons**, each with
$$E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda},\qquad p = \dfrac{h\nu}{c} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}$$
where $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}$ J s (Planck’s constant).
bullets: All photons of one frequency have the **same energy**; brighter light means **more photons** per second, not bigger photons.
Photons travel at $c$ in vacuum, have zero rest mass and are electrically neutral.
In collisions, energy and momentum are conserved; a photon can be absorbed or created.

slides.narration: In the photon picture, light of frequency nu arrives as packets each carrying energy h nu and momentum h over lambda. A brighter lamp of the same colour sends more photons each second, but every photon is the same. Photons move at the speed of light, have no rest mass and no charge. When a photon meets an electron it is either absorbed completely or not at all.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: counting photons
slides.body_md: (a) Find the energy of a photon of 500 nm light in J and eV. (b) A 3.0 mW laser pointer emits light of wavelength 633 nm. How many photons does it emit each second?
bullets: (a) $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{500 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 3.98 \times 10^{-19}$ J $= \dfrac{3.98 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 2.49$ eV.

slides.narration: A green photon carries about four times ten to the minus nineteen joule, or about two and a half electronvolts. That is tiny, so even a weak laser pointer of three milliwatts sends out nearly ten million billion photons every second. With so many, the beam looks perfectly smooth, which is why the particle nature of light went unnoticed for so long.

slides.heading: Einstein’s photoelectric equation
slides.body_md:
One photon gives **all** its energy to **one** electron. Part is used to escape (at least $\varphi_0$); the rest is kinetic energy:
$$h
u = \varphi_0 + K_	ext{max},\qquad K_	ext{max} = eV_0 = h
u - \varphi_0 = h(
u - 
u_0)$$
bullets: Threshold: $h\nu_0 = \varphi_0$, i.e. $\lambda_0 = hc/\varphi_0$.
Electrons from deeper inside lose more energy on the way out, so most have less than $K_\text{max}$.

slides.narration: Einstein’s idea is simple. A single photon is absorbed by a single electron. The electron spends at least the work function to get out, and whatever is left is its kinetic energy. The fastest electrons, from right at the surface, have h nu minus phi nought. If h nu is less than the work function, no electron can escape, whatever the number of photons.

slides.heading: The equation explains every observation
slides.body_md: Using $K_\text{max} = h\nu - \varphi_0$:
bullets: $K_\text{max}$ depends only on $\nu$ (and the metal), not on the number of photons.
$V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}\nu - \dfrac{\varphi_0}{e}$: a straight line of slope $h/e$.
One photon acts at once: no waiting.

slides.narration: Check each observation. More intense light means more photons, so more electrons, but each photon is the same, so the maximum kinetic energy does not change. Below the threshold no single photon has enough energy. The stopping potential is h over e times nu minus phi nought over e, a straight line with slope h over e. And a photon delivers its energy in one go, so there is no time lag.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: potassium in violet light
slides.body_md: Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on potassium ($\varphi_0 = 2.25$ eV). Find the photon energy, $K_\text{max}$, the stopping potential and the threshold wavelength. (Use $hc = 1243$ eV nm.)
bullets: Step 1 — $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1243}{400} \approx 3.11$ eV.
Step 2 — $K_\text{max} = 3.11 - 2.25 \approx 0.86$ eV, so $V_0 \approx 0.86$ V.
Step 3 — $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\varphi_0} = \dfrac{1243}{2.25} \approx 553$ nm.

slides.heading: Wave–particle duality and de Broglie waves
slides.body_md:
Light behaves as a **wave** (interference, diffraction) and as **particles** (photoelectric effect). de Broglie (1924) proposed that **material particles** also have a wave nature, with wavelength
$$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}$$
bullets: For everyday objects $\lambda$ is far too small to detect; for electrons it is comparable to atomic spacings.
The wave and particle pictures are complementary: an experiment shows one or the other.

visual.alt: Flow: light behaves as a wave and as photons; by symmetry matter, known as particles, also behaves as waves of wavelength h over p

slides.narration: Light shows both faces: it interferes like a wave and knocks out electrons like a stream of particles. De Broglie argued that nature should be symmetric, so a moving particle should have a wavelength too, Planck’s constant divided by its momentum. For a cricket ball this is absurdly small, but for an electron it is about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, small but measurable.

slides.heading: Electrons accelerated through a potential
slides.body_md:
An electron accelerated from rest through $V$ gains $K = eV$, so $p = \sqrt{2m_e eV}$ and
$$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m_e eV}} \approx \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{nm}$$
bullets: In general $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$: for equal kinetic energy, a heavier particle has a shorter wavelength.
Higher voltage gives a shorter wavelength: the idea behind the electron microscope.

visual.alt: de Broglie wavelength of an electron against accelerating potential: the wavelength falls as one over the square root of the potential, to about 0.12 nanometre at 100 volts
visual.caption: λ = h/√(2meV) ≈ 1.227/√V nm.

slides.narration: For an electron accelerated through a potential difference V, its kinetic energy is e V and its momentum is root two m e V. Putting in the constants gives a wavelength of one point two two seven divided by root V nanometres. At one hundred volts that is about point one two nanometre, similar to X-ray wavelengths. Electron microscopes use this to see far finer detail than light can.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: an electron and a cricket ball
slides.body_md: Find the de Broglie wavelength of (a) an electron accelerated from rest through 100 V, (b) a cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg moving at 30 m s$^{-1}$.
bullets: (a) $p = \sqrt{2m_e eV} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 100} \approx 5.40 \times 10^{-24}$ kg m s$^{-1}$; $\lambda = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{5.40 \times 10^{-24}} \approx 1.23 \times 10^{-10}$ m (0.123 nm).
(b) $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{0.15 \times 30} \approx 1.47 \times 10^{-34}$ m: far too small ever to detect.

visual.alt: de Broglie wavelength of an electron against accelerating potential: the wavelength falls as one over the square root of the potential, to about 0.12 nanometre at 100 volts
visual.caption: λ = h/√(2meV) ≈ 1.227/√V nm.

slides.narration: For the electron, the momentum is about five point four times ten to the minus twenty four, and dividing Planck’s constant by it gives about point one two three nanometre, the size of an atom. For the cricket ball, the momentum is four point five, and the wavelength is about ten to the minus thirty four metre, unimaginably smaller than a nucleus. That is why we never notice the wave nature of everyday objects.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: proton or electron?
slides.body_md: A proton ($m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg) and an electron have the same kinetic energy. Find the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths, $\lambda_e/\lambda_p$.
bullets: Step 1 — $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$, so with equal $K$, $\dfrac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p}{m_e}}$.
Step 2 — $\sqrt{\dfrac{1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}} \approx 42.8$: the electron’s wavelength is about 43 times longer.

visual.alt: de Broglie wavelength of an electron against accelerating potential: the wavelength falls as one over the square root of the potential, to about 0.12 nanometre at 100 volts
visual.caption: λ = h/√(2meV) ≈ 1.227/√V nm.

slides.narration: With the same kinetic energy, momentum grows as the square root of mass, so the wavelength falls as one over root mass. The proton is about eighteen hundred and thirty five times heavier than the electron, and the square root of that is about forty three. So the electron’s wavelength is about forty three times the proton’s. For equal momentum, by contrast, the wavelengths would be equal.

sections.body_md:
- **Work function** $\varphi_0$: least energy needed to free an electron from a metal surface; 1 eV = $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ J. Emission by heat (thermionic), strong field (field emission) or light (photoelectric).

- Zinc and cadmium need UV; alkali metals (Na, K, Cs) respond to visible light.

sections.heading: 2. Experimental study
sections.body_md:
Emitter C and collector A in an evacuated tube; light through a quartz window; collector potential variable and reversible; microammeter for the photocurrent.
- **Intensity:** photocurrent ∝ intensity (number of electrons per second ∝ intensity).
- **Potential:** current rises to a **saturation** value as A is made positive; it falls to zero at the **stopping potential** $-V_0$: $eV_0 = K_\text{max}$. Different intensities, same ν: different saturation currents, **same** $V_0$.
- **Frequency:** same intensity, higher ν: same saturation current, **larger** $V_0$. $V_0$ against ν is a straight line cutting the axis at the **threshold frequency** $\nu_0$; slope $h/e$ for all metals.
- **No time lag** (< $10^{-9}$ s).
- **Wave theory fails:** it predicts $K_\text{max}$ rising with intensity, emission at any frequency, and a time lag in dim light.

key_terms.definition_md: The negative collector potential that just stops the most energetic photoelectrons; eV₀ = K_max.
Minimum frequency of light that can cause photoelectric emission from a given metal.
Maximum photocurrent, reached when all emitted electrons are collected.

u = \varphi_0 + K_	ext{max}$, i.e. $K_	ext{max} = eV_0 = h
u - \varphi_0 = h(
u - 
u_0)$.

u_0 = \varphi_0/h$, $\lambda_0 = hc/\varphi_0$.
- $V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}
u - \dfrac{\varphi_0}{e}$: slope $h/e$ (same for all metals), intercept $

sections.heading: 4. Matter waves
sections.body_md:
- **Dual nature:** radiation shows wave (interference, diffraction) and particle (photoelectric effect) behaviour.
- **de Broglie relation:** a particle of momentum $p$ has wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$.
- Charged particle accelerated through $V$: $K = qV$, $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$; electron: $\lambda \approx \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}$ nm.
- Equal kinetic energy: $\lambda \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$. Equal momentum: equal $\lambda$.
- Everyday objects: $\lambda$ far too small to observe; electrons: comparable to atomic spacings (basis of the electron microscope).

questions.stem_md: An uncharged zinc plate, insulated from the ground, is exposed to ultraviolet light for some time. The plate becomes

options.text_md: negatively charged, because it gains electrons from the light
positively charged, because it gains protons
still uncharged, because light carries no charge
positively charged, because it loses electrons

questions.solution_md: Ultraviolet light ejects photoelectrons from zinc; losing negative charge leaves the plate positive — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal is called its work ___.
questions.solution_md: The work **function** φ₀, usually given in electronvolts.

questions.stem_md: The work function of zinc is 4.3 eV. Express it in joules, in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J (3 significant figures).
Match each scientist in Column A with the observation or idea in Column B.

options.text_md: Hertz
Hallwachs
Lenard
Einstein

match_right.text_md: A negatively charged zinc plate lost its charge in ultraviolet light
Light energy is absorbed in packets of size hν
Ultraviolet light helped sparks jump across a gap
Light on the emitter of an evacuated tube produced a current

questions.solution_md: Hertz → sparks (1 → r); Hallwachs → zinc plate (2 → p); Lenard → current in an evacuated tube (3 → s); Einstein → packets hν (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: Which of these metals can emit photoelectrons when lit by ordinary visible light?

options.text_md: Zinc
Copper
Potassium
Platinum

questions.solution_md: Alkali metals such as potassium have work functions near 2 eV, within the energy of visible photons; zinc, copper and platinum need ultraviolet — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Hertz found that sparks jumped across a gap more easily when the electrodes were lit by ultraviolet light.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. This 1887 observation was the first sign of the photoelectric effect.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A positively charged zinc plate does not lose its charge when exposed to ultraviolet light.

**Reason (R):** Any photoelectrons emitted from a positively charged plate are attracted back to it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: the positive plate pulls the ejected electrons back, so it keeps its charge — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the photoelectric experiment, why is the tube containing the emitter and collector evacuated, and why is its window made of quartz?

answer.model_answer_md: The tube is **evacuated** so that photoelectrons travel from emitter to collector **without colliding** with gas molecules, which would slow or stop them and produce ions. The window is made of **quartz** because ordinary glass **absorbs ultraviolet** light, which many metals need for emission; quartz lets it through.

questions.solution_md: No collisions; quartz transmits UV.

marking_scheme.step: Vacuum: no collisions with gas molecules

questions.stem_md: Light of a fixed frequency above the threshold falls on a photocell. If its intensity is doubled,

options.text_md: the saturation current and the stopping potential both double
the saturation current doubles and the stopping potential is unchanged
the stopping potential doubles and the saturation current is unchanged
neither the saturation current nor the stopping potential changes

questions.solution_md: Twice as many photons free twice as many electrons, but each photon has the same energy, so K_max and V₀ do not change — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Graphs of stopping potential against frequency are drawn for two different metals. The two lines

options.text_md: are parallel, with slope h/e, but cut the frequency axis at different points
have different slopes but the same intercept
coincide
are parallel to the frequency axis

questions.solution_md: V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ₀/e: the slope h/e is universal; the intercept ν₀ = φ₀/h depends on the metal — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Light of frequency below the threshold frequency cannot eject photoelectrons, however intense it is.

**Reason (R):** The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons increases with the intensity of the light.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: K_max depends on the frequency, not on the intensity — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The stopping potential for photoelectrons from a metal is 2.0 V. Find the maximum speed of the photoelectrons, in units of 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\tfrac{1}{2}m v_\text{max}^2 = eV_0$, so $v_\text{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2eV_0}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2.0}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}} \approx 8.39 \times 10^{5}$ m s$^{-1}$, i.e. $\dfrac{8.39 \times 10^{5}}{10^{5}} = 8.39$.

questions.stem_md: Photoelectrons are just stopped by a retarding potential of 0.75 V. Find their maximum kinetic energy, in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Two curves of photocurrent against collector potential are obtained with light of the same intensity but different frequencies. The curve for the higher frequency

options.text_md: reaches a higher saturation current and the same stopping potential
reaches a lower saturation current and the same stopping potential
reaches the same saturation current but cuts the potential axis at a more negative value
cuts the potential axis at a less negative value

questions.solution_md: Same intensity gives the same saturation current (idealised); higher frequency gives larger K_max and so a larger stopping potential — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? For light of a fixed frequency above the threshold, doubling the intensity doubles the stopping potential.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The stopping potential depends only on the frequency (and the metal); intensity changes only the number of photoelectrons.

questions.stem_md: When light of frequency above the threshold first falls on a metal, photoelectric emission begins

options.text_md: only after a delay that is longer for dimmer light
after about one second, whatever the intensity
only once the metal has warmed up
almost at once, within about 10⁻⁹ s, even in very dim light

questions.solution_md: There is no measurable time lag; each photon gives its energy to an electron at once — option (d).

questions.stem_md: State three observations of the photoelectric effect that cannot be explained by the wave theory of light, giving for each what the wave theory would predict.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **K_max is independent of intensity**; a wave of greater intensity should give electrons more energy. (2) There is a **threshold frequency** below which no emission occurs, however intense the light; on the wave theory any frequency should work if the light is bright enough. (3) Emission is **instantaneous**; a wave spreads its energy thinly, so in dim light an electron should need a **long time** to gather enough energy.

questions.solution_md: Intensity, threshold, time lag.

marking_scheme.step: K_max independent of intensity, with wave prediction
No time lag, with wave prediction

questions.stem_md: Sketch (describe) the graph of photocurrent against collector potential (a) for two intensities I₁ < I₂ of light of the same frequency, (b) for two frequencies ν₁ < ν₂ of light of the same intensity. Point out what is common in each case.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Both curves start from zero at the **same stopping potential** $-V_0$, rise, and level off; the I₂ curve levels off at a **higher saturation current**. Common: the **stopping potential**. (b) Both curves level off at the **same saturation current**, but the ν₂ curve starts from a **more negative** stopping potential. Common: the **saturation current**.

questions.solution_md: Intensity changes saturation; frequency changes stopping potential.

marking_scheme.step: (b) same saturation, larger V₀ for ν₂
Common quantity named in each case

questions.stem_md: Why does the photocurrent stop increasing (saturate) when the collector potential is made more and more positive?

answer.model_answer_md: The number of electrons **emitted per second** is fixed by the **intensity** of the light. Once the collector is positive enough to collect **all** of them, a higher potential cannot increase the number arriving per second, so the current stays at its **saturation** value.

questions.solution_md: All emitted electrons already collected.

marking_scheme.step: All electrons collected: current cannot rise further

questions.stem_md: As the retarding potential on the collector is increased from zero, the photocurrent falls gradually rather than suddenly. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Photoelectrons leave the metal with a **range of kinetic energies**, from zero up to $K_\text{max}$, because electrons from below the surface lose different amounts of energy on the way out. A small retarding potential turns back only the **slowest** electrons; larger potentials stop more of them, until at $V_0$ even the **fastest** are stopped.

questions.solution_md: Spread of electron energies.

marking_scheme.step: Electrons emitted with a range of energies up to K_max
Increasing potential stops more of them, all at V₀

questions.stem_md: Suppose light were a classical wave. Light of intensity 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻² falls on a metal of work function 2.3 eV, and each electron can absorb energy only over an area of about 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ m². Estimate how long, in days, an electron would take to gather enough energy to escape (3 significant figures). (In experiments, emission is immediate.)
questions.solution_md: Power per electron $= IA = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-19} = 2.0 \times 10^{-25}$ W. Energy needed $= 2.3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 3.68 \times 10^{-19}$ J. Time $t = \dfrac{3.68 \times 10^{-19}}{2.0 \times 10^{-25}} = 1.84 \times 10^{6}$ s, i.e. $\dfrac{1.84 \times 10^{6}}{86400} = 21.3$ days.

questions.stem_md: In a photoelectric experiment, light of frequency 9.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz gives a stopping potential of 1.62 V and light of 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz gives 0.38 V. Find Planck’s constant from these data, in units of 10⁻³⁴ J s (3 significant figures).

marking_scheme.step: Subtract the two Einstein equations: e ΔV₀ = h Δν

questions.stem_md: Photons of energy 4.0 eV fall on a metal whose work function is 2.5 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, in eV.
questions.solution_md: $K_\text{max} = h\nu - \varphi_0 = 4.0 - 2.5 = 1.5$ eV.

questions.stem_md: Find the energy of a photon of red light of wavelength 620 nm, in eV (3 significant figures). (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)
questions.solution_md: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{620 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 3.21 \times 10^{-19}$ J, i.e. $\dfrac{3.21 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.01$ eV.

questions.stem_md: The work function of a metal is 2.0 eV. Find its threshold frequency, in units of 10¹⁴ Hz (3 significant figures).
A metal has a work function of 3.0 eV. Find its threshold wavelength, in nm (3 significant figures). (Take hc = 1243 eV nm.)
questions.solution_md: $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\varphi_0} = \dfrac{1243}{3.0} \approx 414$ nm.

questions.stem_md: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 250 nm falls on a metal of work function 4.2 eV. Find the stopping potential, in volts (2 significant figures). (hc = 1243 eV nm.)
questions.solution_md: $h\nu = \dfrac{1243}{250} \approx 4.97$ eV; $eV_0 = h\nu - \varphi_0 = 4.97 - 4.2 = 0.77$ eV, so $V_0 \approx 0.77$ V.

questions.stem_md: When light of wavelength 300 nm falls on a metal, the stopping potential is 1.4 V. Find the work function of the metal, in eV (3 significant figures). (hc = 1243 eV nm.)
A sodium street lamp radiates 10 W of yellow light of wavelength 589 nm. How many photons does it emit per second? Give the answer in units of 10¹⁹ (3 significant figures).
True or false? A brighter beam of light of the same colour consists of photons of greater energy.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Every photon of a given frequency has energy hν; a brighter beam simply carries more photons per second.

questions.stem_md: Find the momentum of a photon of wavelength 500 nm, in units of 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹ (3 significant figures).
Very intense orange light of wavelength 600 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.5 eV. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: No photoelectrons are emitted, because each photon has only about 2.1 eV
Photoelectrons are emitted because the light is very intense
Photoelectrons are emitted after a short delay
Photoelectrons are emitted with zero kinetic energy

questions.solution_md: hν = 1243/600 ≈ 2.07 eV < 2.5 eV: no single photon can free an electron, whatever the intensity — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Light of frequency ν ejects photoelectrons from a metal. If the frequency is doubled (still with the same metal), the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons becomes

options.text_md: exactly double
less than double but more than before
more than double its earlier value
unchanged

questions.solution_md: K₁ = hν − φ₀; K₂ = 2hν − φ₀ = 2K₁ + φ₀ > 2K₁ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The same ultraviolet light falls on caesium (φ₀ ≈ 2.1 eV) and on zinc (φ₀ ≈ 4.3 eV), and both emit photoelectrons. Which gives the larger stopping potential?

options.text_md: Zinc, because its work function is larger
Both the same, because the light is the same
Zinc, because zinc needs ultraviolet light
Caesium, because its work function is smaller

questions.solution_md: eV₀ = hν − φ₀; with the same hν, the smaller φ₀ leaves more kinetic energy — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons does not depend on the intensity of the incident light.

**Reason (R):** Each photoelectron is ejected by absorbing a single photon, whose energy depends only on the frequency of the light.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: one photon per electron, and every photon of frequency ν has energy hν — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The stopping potential for a given frequency of light is different for different metals.

**Reason (R):** The momentum of a photon is h/λ.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A; A follows from eV₀ = hν − φ₀ with φ₀ depending on the metal — option (b).

Einstein: $K_	ext{max} = h

u \ge \varphi_0$, i.e. $
u \ge

questions.solution_md: Apply K_max = hν − φ₀ with one photon per electron.

questions.stem_md: Graphs of stopping potential against frequency for two metals are parallel straight lines. What does the common slope give, and what does the intercept on the frequency axis give?

answer.model_answer_md:
From $eV_0 = h
u - \varphi_0$, $V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}
u - \dfrac{\varphi_0}{e}$. The **slope** is $h/e$, the same for all metals, so it gives **Planck’s constant**. The **intercept** on the ν axis is the **threshold frequency** $

questions.stem_md: The threshold wavelength of a metal is 550 nm. Ultraviolet light of wavelength 330 nm falls on it. Find (a) the work function, (b) the stopping potential, (c) the maximum speed of the photoelectrons. (hc = 1243 eV nm, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\varphi_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{1243}{550} \approx 2.26$ eV.
(b) $h\nu = \dfrac{1243}{330} \approx 3.77$ eV; $K_\text{max} = 3.77 - 2.26 \approx 1.51$ eV, so $V_0 \approx 1.51$ V.
(c) $v_\text{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K_\text{max}}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.51 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}} \approx 7.28 \times 10^{5}$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: φ₀ = hc/λ₀; K = hν − φ₀; v = √(2K/m).

questions.stem_md: Light of wavelength 400 nm and then of 600 nm falls on a metal of work function 1.8 eV. Find the ratio of the maximum speeds of the photoelectrons in the two cases, v₄₀₀/v₆₀₀ (3 significant figures). (hc = 1243 eV nm.)
Using the photon picture, explain why doubling the intensity of light of a fixed frequency (above threshold) doubles the photocurrent.

answer.model_answer_md: For a fixed frequency every photon has the same energy $h\nu$, so doubling the intensity means **twice as many photons** strike the metal each second. Each photon can free **one** electron, so about **twice as many photoelectrons** are emitted per second, and the photocurrent doubles.

questions.solution_md: Intensity ∝ number of photons.

marking_scheme.step: Doubling intensity doubles the photon rate
One photon frees one electron: current doubles

questions.stem_md: The potential difference that accelerates an electron from rest is made four times as large. Its de Broglie wavelength becomes

options.text_md: half as large
one quarter as large
twice as large
four times as large

questions.solution_md: λ = h/√(2meV) ∝ 1/√V; √4 = 2, so λ halves — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through 400 V, in picometres (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m eV}} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 400}} \approx 6.14 \times 10^{-11}$ m, i.e. $6.14 \times 10^{-11} \times 10^{12} = 61.4$ pm.

questions.stem_md: A proton (mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 2.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Find its de Broglie wavelength, in picometres (3 significant figures).
An electron, a proton and an alpha particle have the same kinetic energy. Which has the longest de Broglie wavelength?

options.text_md: The proton
The electron
The alpha particle
All have the same wavelength

questions.solution_md: λ = h/√(2mK): for equal K, the lightest particle has the longest wavelength — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An electron and a proton moving with the same momentum have the same de Broglie wavelength.

**Reason (R):** The de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p depends only on the momentum of the particle.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: equal p gives equal h/p, whatever the masses — option (a).

questions.stem_md: We do not observe wave effects such as diffraction for a moving cricket ball because

options.text_md: its de Broglie wavelength is far smaller than any object or opening it meets
it has no de Broglie wavelength because it is not charged
its de Broglie wavelength is far larger than the ball
only particles moving near the speed of light have a wavelength

questions.solution_md: λ = h/mv is about 10⁻³⁴ m for a ball: far too small for any diffraction to be seen — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Through what potential difference must an electron, starting from rest, be accelerated so that its de Broglie wavelength is 0.10 nm? Give the answer in volts (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} \Rightarrow V = \dfrac{h^2}{2me\lambda^2} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})^2}{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times (1.0 \times 10^{-10})^2} \approx 151$ V.

questions.stem_md: A proton and an alpha particle (mass 4m_p, charge 2e) are each accelerated from rest through the same potential difference. Find the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths, λ_p/λ_α (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $K = qV$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$ and $\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_\alpha q_\alpha}{m_p q_p}} = \sqrt{4 \times 2} = 2.83$.

questions.stem_md: A photon and an electron both have a wavelength of 1.0 nm. Find the ratio of the photon’s energy to the electron’s kinetic energy (3 significant figures). (hc = 1243 eV nm; h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.)
questions.solution_md: Photon: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1243}{1.0} = 1243$ eV. Electron: $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = 6.63 \times 10^{-25}$ kg m s$^{-1}$, $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m} = \dfrac{(6.63 \times 10^{-25})^2}{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31}} \approx 2.42 \times 10^{-19}$ J $= \dfrac{2.42 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 1.51$ eV. Ratio $= \dfrac{1243}{1.51} \approx 824$.

marking_scheme.step: Photon 1243 eV; electron K = p²/2m ≈ 1.51 eV

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the dual nature of radiation? State de Broglie’s hypothesis.

answer.model_answer_md: Radiation shows **wave** properties (interference, diffraction) in some experiments and **particle** properties (photons in the photoelectric effect) in others: this is its **dual nature**. **de Broglie** proposed that moving **material particles** also have a wave nature, with wavelength $\lambda = h/p = h/mv$.

questions.solution_md: Wave and particle; λ = h/p for matter.

marking_scheme.step: de Broglie: λ = h/p for particles

questions.stem_md: A slow neutron (mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) has a kinetic energy of 0.025 eV. Find its de Broglie wavelength, in nm (3 significant figures).
An electron and a proton have the same de Broglie wavelength. Compare (a) their momenta, (b) their speeds, (c) their kinetic energies.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\lambda = h/p$, so equal $\lambda$ means **equal momenta**.
(b) $v = p/m$, so $\dfrac{v_e}{v_p} = \dfrac{m_p}{m_e} \approx 1835$: the electron is about 1835 times faster.
(c) $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so $\dfrac{K_e}{K_p} = \dfrac{m_p}{m_e} \approx 1835$: the electron has the greater kinetic energy.

questions.solution_md: Equal p; v and K ∝ 1/m.

questions.stem_md: For electrons accelerated from rest through a potential difference V, a graph of de Broglie wavelength λ against 1/√V is

options.text_md: a parabola
a straight line through the origin
a straight line parallel to the 1/√V axis
a curve that falls as 1/√V increases

questions.solution_md: λ = h/√(2meV) = (h/√(2me)) × (1/√V): λ is proportional to 1/√V — option (b).

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe an experimental arrangement to study the photoelectric effect. (b) Describe, with graphs (described in words), how the photocurrent depends on (i) the intensity of light, (ii) the collector potential, and (iii) the frequency of light. (c) State two observations that show light cannot be treated only as a wave.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An evacuated glass tube with a quartz window contains a photosensitive emitter plate C and a collector plate A. Light of known frequency and intensity falls on C. A battery with a reversing key and a potential divider sets the potential of A relative to C (read on a voltmeter), and a microammeter in series measures the photocurrent.

(b)(i) Photocurrent against intensity: a **straight line through the origin**. (ii) Photocurrent against collector potential: rises to a **saturation** value for positive potentials and falls to zero at the **stopping potential** $-V_0$; higher intensity gives a higher saturation current but the **same** $V_0$. (iii) Higher frequency at the same intensity: same saturation current, **larger** $V_0$; $V_0$ against ν is a **straight line** meeting the ν axis at the threshold $\nu_0$.

(c) Any two: $K_\text{max}$ is independent of intensity; no emission below $\nu_0$ however intense the light; emission is instantaneous.

questions.solution_md: Set-up; three dependences; failures of the wave theory.

marking_scheme.step: Arrangement with emitter, collector, variable potential, meters
Saturation and stopping potential; same V₀ for different intensities
Effect of frequency: V₀ rises linearly, threshold ν₀
Two observations against the wave picture

(b) Use it to show that the graph of stopping potential against frequency is a straight line, and state what its slope and its intercept on the frequency axis represent. (c) Blue light of wavelength 450 nm falls on a surface of work function 2.3 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, the stopping potential, the threshold frequency and the threshold wavelength. (hc = 1243 eV nm, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.)

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md: (a) State de Broglie’s relation. (b) Show that the de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m and charge q accelerated from rest through a potential difference V is λ = h/√(2mqV), and hence that for an electron λ ≈ 1.227/√V nm. (c) Find the wavelength of an electron accelerated through 150 V, and of a proton accelerated through the same potential difference. (d) Why can electrons of this energy be diffracted by crystals while protons of the same energy are much harder to diffract?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A particle of momentum $p$ has wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}$.

(b) Gain in kinetic energy $K = qV = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so $p = \sqrt{2mqV}$ and $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$. For an electron: $\dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}} \approx 1.23 \times 10^{-9}$ m V$^{1/2}$, so $\lambda \approx \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}$ nm.

(c) Electron: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m_e eV}} \approx 1.00 \times 10^{-10}$ m (about 0.100 nm). Proton: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m_p eV}} \approx 2.34 \times 10^{-12}$ m, about 43 times smaller.

(d) The electron’s wavelength (about 0.1 nm) is comparable to the spacing of atoms in a crystal, so the crystal acts as a diffraction grating; the proton’s wavelength is about 43 times smaller, so diffraction effects are far weaker.

questions.solution_md: λ = h/p, K = qV.

questions.stem_md: (a) State four properties of photons. (b) A 5.0 mW red laser emits light of wavelength 650 nm. Find the energy of each photon (in J and eV) and the number of photons emitted per second. (c) The beam falls on a surface of work function 2.0 eV. Will photoelectrons be emitted? If so, find their maximum kinetic energy. (d) How would the photocurrent and the maximum kinetic energy change if a 10 mW laser of the same wavelength were used?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Any four: energy $E = h\nu$; momentum $p = h/\lambda$; speed $c$ in vacuum; zero rest mass; no charge; intensity of light ∝ number of photons per second; energy and momentum conserved in collisions.

(b) $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{650 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 3.06 \times 10^{-19}$ J $\approx 1.91$ eV. $N = \dfrac{P}{E} = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-3}}{3.06 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 1.63 \times 10^{16}$ s$^{-1}$.

(c) **No.** Each photon has only about $1.91$ eV, less than the work function of 2.0 eV, and one photon must free one electron, so no photoelectrons are emitted.

(d) A 10 mW laser sends **twice as many** photons per second, but each still has about $1.91$ eV, below 2.0 eV. There is **still no emission**: the photocurrent stays zero and there is no kinetic energy to speak of. Only light of shorter wavelength (below $1243/2.0 \approx 622$ nm) would work.

questions.solution_md: E = hc/λ; N = P/E; Einstein.

marking_scheme.step: 10 mW: more photons but still no emission; need λ < 622 nm
